articles.title: Moradores de 52 cidades do ES vão poder usar sinal de outras operadora | G1
articles.standfirst: Resolução da Anatel permite que o celular se conecte automaticamente a redes concorrentes em áreas sem cobertura; medida beneficia 67% dos municípios capixabas sem custo adicional para o consumidor.
articles.summary: Resolução da Anatel permite que o celular se conecte automaticamente a redes concorrentes em áreas sem cobertura; medida beneficia 67% dos municípios capixabas sem custo adicional.
articles.body:
Novas regras de roaming nacional foram aprovadas pela Anatel — Foto: Marcello Casal jr/Agência Brasil

Uma nova regra de roaming nacional vai permitir que celulares se conectem sozinhos às redes de operadoras concorrentes em locais sem sinal . A mudança, aprovada pela Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel), vai beneficiar moradores de 52 cidades do Espírito Santo sem cobrar nenhum valor extra no plano de telefone (veja lista abaixo) .

A resolução foi publicada no dia 9 de novembro e entra em vigor em dezembro deste ano . O objetivo, segundo o Ministério das Comunicações, é ampliar as possibilidades de conexão em municípios com menos de 30 mil habitantes, localidades fora das sedes municipais e rodovias federais e estaduais.

🔍 O roaming (itinerância) é a tecnologia que permite ao seu celular usar a rede de outras operadoras para fazer ligações, enviar mensagens e acessar a internet quando você está fora da área de cobertura da sua própria operadora.

A nova regra define que a troca de sinal aconteça de forma automática. Na prática, quando o consumidor entrar em um local onde a própria operadora não tem cobertura, o celular irá buscar e se conectar na rede de outra empresa disponível.

A conexão será realizada sem necessidade de trocar de chip. Além disso, a Anatel proibiu qualquer cobrança adicional para o uso da tecnologia.

Mais de 50 cidades do Espírito Santo podem ser beneficiadas

A nova regra vai beneficiar municípios com menos de 30 mil habitantes.

No Espírito Santo, segundo estimativas populacionais do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) para 2026, 52 das 78 cidades se enquadram no perfil inicial da medida — o que representa cerca de 67% dos municípios capixabas.

A Anatel informou que a expectativa inicial é de que todas as sedes municipais brasileiras com menos de 30 mil habitantes sejam beneficiadas. No entanto, a agência ainda vai divulgar a lista definitiva das áreas contempladas, que também incluirá localidades fora das sedes municipais e trechos de rodovias.

A obrigação de compartilhamento será aplicada às redes de telefonia móvel instaladas para cumprir compromissos de cobertura e expansão estabelecidos pela Anatel ou que tenham recebido financiamento, total ou parcial, do setor público federal.

A lista inclui cidades de diferentes regiões capixabas. Veja as cidades:

A norma entrará em vigor em 9 de dezembro de 2026. No entanto, segundo a Anatel, a liberação do sinal vai ocorrer em três fases:

9 de março de 2027: primeira etapa, voltada aos municípios com menos de 30 mil moradores.

8 de maio de 2027: segunda etapa, abrangendo comunidades e áreas fora do centro das cidades.

7 de julho de 2027: terceira etapa, contemplando trechos de estradas federais e estaduais.

As operadoras receberam a obrigação de assinar acordos de compartilhamento sem exclusividade entre si.

Em nota, a Conexis Brasil Digital, associação das maiores operadoras de telecomunicação do país, afirmou que “as associadas cumprem as determinações da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) e ainda avaliam a resolução que estabelece novas regras de roaming”.

articles.title: Alunos de escola rural batem recorde com foguete que atingiu 401 m | G1
articles.standfirst: Estudantes de Ribas do Rio Pardo alcançaram 401 metros, maior distância entre as 86 equipes participantes da 97ª Jornada Nacional de Foguetes; nove alunos representaram a escola na competição nacional.
articles.summary: Estudantes de Ribas do Rio Pardo alcançaram 401 metros, maior distância entre as 86 equipes participantes da 97ª Jornada Nacional de Foguetes.
articles.body:
Alunos da Escola Municipal Usina do Mimoso Polo – Extensão Modelo 2, da zona rural de Ribas do Rio Pardo , conquistaram três medalhas de ouro na 97ª Jornada Nacional de Foguetes, realizada em Barra do Piraí (RJ). Um dos foguetes lançados pelos estudantes atingiu 401 metros, a maior distância registrada entre as 86 equipes participantes desta edição.

Orientados pelo professor Jackson Lenon da Silva Pais, os estudantes participaram da competição com três equipes, cada uma formada por três alunos. Ao todo, a escola levou seis foguetes para os lançamentos, dos quais três conquistaram medalhas de ouro.

Os alunos do 6º ao 9º ano competiram no nível 3 da olimpíada, modalidade que utiliza foguetes construídos com garrafas PET e impulsionados por ar e água. O evento aconteceu entre os dias 9 e 12 de novembro.

Alunos receberam três medalhas de ouro na competição. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

As três equipes da escola obtiveram os seguintes resultados:

Equipe 34: 315 metros, com Guilherme Petronilio Morendi, Bianca Vitória Ferreira dos Anjos e Eliza Beatriz Rodrigues Araújo.

Equipe 35: 316 metros, com Pietro Eduardo Alves Rodrigues Antônio, Luis Carlos dos Santos Cogo e Giovana Cardoso Rogério.

Equipe 36: 401 metros, com Henzo Gabriel da Silva Gomes, Sarah Thalia Nunes Leal e Sofia da Silva Fagundes.

Segundo o professor Jackson Pais, os lançamentos ocorreram em dois dias. Cada equipe teve direito a uma tentativa na terça-feira e outra na quarta-feira. Para a classificação, foi considerada a maior distância alcançada por cada grupo.

Para o g1 , o professor afirmou que os resultados representam mais do que medalhas e recordes de distância. Segundo ele, os resultados são motivo de orgulho, especialmente pela dedicação dos estudantes e pelas condições em que o projeto foi desenvolvido.

"É algo excepcional. Um trabalho em zona rural, com alunos que teoricamente são um pouco limitados na questão de conhecimento territorial, ir pro Rio de Janeiro, treinar incansavelmente, com um professor chato, que busca perfeição. Chegarem lá e fazerem bonito do jeito que fizeram, né? Como que não vou me sentir orgulhoso? Até agora a ficha não caiu", relata.

Segundo Jackson, o projeto também busca mostrar aos estudantes que a localização da escola não limita as oportunidades de aprendizagem nem a participação em competições nacionais.

“Nosso maior objetivo é mostrar aos alunos que o lugar onde eles estudam não determina até onde podem chegar. Somos uma escola pública rural e conseguimos competir nacionalmente, conquistar títulos e demonstrar que nossos estudantes têm capacidade de alcançar resultados extraordinários”, destaca.

O trabalho teve início em 2025, quando o professor passou a incentivar os alunos a participar da Olimpíada Brasileira de Astronomia e Astronáutica (OBA) e da Olimpíada Brasileira de Foguetes (OBAFOG).

Naquele ano, duas equipes da escola conseguiram classificação para a Jornada Nacional de Foguetes. Na estreia, uma conquistou medalha de prata, com lançamento de 47 metros, e a outra recebeu menção honrosa.

Em 2026, após intensificar os treinamentos e aprimorar a construção dos foguetes, a escola classificou três equipes para a etapa nacional. Os alunos fizeram ajustes na estrutura, nas aletas e na distribuição de peso dos equipamentos para melhorar a estabilidade e o alcance.

Além dos resultados na competição de foguetes, a escola também teve destaque na OBA de 2026. O estudante Guilherme Petronilio Morendi, do 9º ano, alcançou nota 9 e a terceira colocação nacional no nível 3, conforme os resultados informados pela escola.

Com o desempenho, recebeu convite para participar da seletiva que escolhe estudantes para representar o Brasil em olimpíadas internacionais de Astronomia. Ele já participou das primeiras etapas do processo.

Após os resultados de 2025 e 2026, a escola pretende dar continuidade às atividades científicas e tecnológicas, com novos treinamentos e experimentos para as próximas edições das olimpíadas.

articles.title: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health
articles.summary: Ten different research teams will look at how well teenagers are coping without social media.
articles.body:
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.

The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.

Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.

The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.

Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.

And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.

Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.

"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.

"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."

Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.

People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay

Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s

Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court

Introduced last December, the social media ban in Australia is yet to produce clear results - with its supporters saying it is successful in protecting young people from harmful content and its critics arguing the ban has been too harsh.

Online forum Reddit and a digital rights group are currently involved in a high court battle in the country, arguing that the law change is unconstitutional.

There have also been reports of Australian teens finding ways to get round the ban - with the UK government promising to make sure tougher blocks are in place.

articles.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit may not end his influence; former CEO can nominate two board directors
articles.summary: Jensen Huang may have stepped away from Nvidia's CEO chair, but he still has some say in who sits on the company's board.
articles.body: Jensen Huang may have stepped away from Nvidia's CEO chair, but he still has some say in who sits on the company's board.The former chief executive has the right to nominate two directors to Nvidia's board ahead of its annual shareholder meeting, according to the company's proxy and corporate filings.Huang's current shareholding makes this possible.He owns roughly 3.5% of Nvidia, while data from LSEG shows that he and entities linked to him have held more than 3% of the company's shares for over three years. Under Nvidia's rules, shareholders or groups holding more than 3% of the voting power for at least three years can nominate directors whose names must be included in the company's proxy materials for the annual shareholder vote.The company's annual meeting typically takes place in June. Huang would be entitled to nominate candidates who qualify as independent board members, putting them forward for consideration by shareholders.The provision could give the Nvidia co-founder a way to retain a degree of influence over the company's future even after leaving the CEO's office. Board members are responsible for selecting company leadership and overseeing its operations, making the nomination right particularly significant as investors, customers and chip industry executives assess Huang's future role.However, the process does not automatically secure board positions for his nominees. Shareholders must approve the candidates through a vote. Nvidia can also leave a nominee out if the individual has violated the company's bylaws and charter.The question of Huang's future involvement comes amid an investigation announced by Nvidia's board on November 8. The board said it had initiated the investigation following recent reporting that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence effort.Reuters could not establish whether Huang's conduct had breached Nvidia's bylaws or charter. The company and a representative for Huang did not respond to requests for comment.Musk, Trump and investors back Huang's return, but board remains firmHuang's resignation last week, following his extramarital affairs, has also triggered calls for him to return as CEO. Elon Musk, employees, investors and US President Donald Trump are among those who have advocated for his return to the leadership position at the chip designer.Despite the support, Nvidia's board was not considering reinstating Huang, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday.Huang, however, has not ruled out returning to the role. In a statement released on Tuesday, he said he "would be honored" to become CEO again if the board believed it would be in the best interests of shareholders and employees.Meanwhile, Nvidia's latest earnings provided some relief for investors. The company issued a quarterly revenue forecast above Wall Street estimates after the market closed on Tuesday, offering some relief following the uncertainty surrounding his exit.Its third-quarter earnings statement, however, made no reference to Huang's departure or the possibility of his return.Nvidia reported revenue of more than $116 billion, double the amount recorded a year earlier and higher than Wall Street estimates. articles.summary: A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison in the US for plotting to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other prominent American
articles.body: A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison in the US for plotting to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other prominent American politicians in 2024 at the behest of Iran, the department of justice said on Tuesday, news agency Reuters reported.Asif Merchant, 48, was sentenced to 330 months in prison by US district judge Eric R Komitee in a federal court in Brooklyn for attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire, the DOJ said.Prosecutors said Merchant attempted to recruit people in the US to carry out the plot targeting Trump and others in retaliation for Washington's killing of Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani in 2020, during Trump's first term.The targets also included then-President Joe Biden and Nikki Haley, who challenged Trump for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024, federal prosecutors said.A federal jury convicted Merchant in March of travelling to the US to arrange political assassinations on American soil, according to the DOJ. His trial began in late February in Brooklyn, days before Trump ordered US-Israeli strikes on Iran that marked the beginning of the Iran war.Merchant testified that he had joined the plot involving Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) unwillingly to protect his family in Tehran. He said he was never instructed to kill a specific person but that his Iranian handler had named three individuals during conversations in the Iranian capital.The plot was thwarted before any attack took place. A person Merchant approached in April 2024 to help carry out the plan reported his activities to law enforcement and became a confidential informant, the DOJ said. Merchant was arrested later that year and pleaded not guilty.Tehran has denied plotting to assassinate Trump or other US officials.US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have killed thousands and displaced millions. articles.title: Netanyahu fumes as Eisenkot bloc installs new Knesset Speaker in Israel with votes of ‘terror supporters’
articles.summary: Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has elected Matan Kahana, a member of Gadi Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party, as its new Speaker, marking a
articles.body: Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has elected Matan Kahana, a member of Gadi Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party, as its new Speaker, marking a significant setback for caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu as rival parties seek to consolidate their control over the legislature.Kahana secured 66 votes against 52 for the rival candidate in Tuesday night’s vote, according to the Knesset spokesperson’s office. He replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party.The election marks an important parliamentary gain for the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc, which has secured control of the speakership despite failing to establish a governing majority following the October 27 general election.Accepting the position, Kahana said: “With great reverence, I now accept the role of speaker of the Knesset of Israel. The Knesset is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, regardless of religion, race, or gender. And I intend to be the speaker for all of them.”Eisenkot welcomed the outcome, describing it as the beginning of a new chapter for the legislature.“I congratulate MK Matan Kahana, my fellow traveller, the incoming Speaker of the Knesset. A new chapter begins. Under Matan, the Knesset will once again become the people’s house—the house of all the people—where every segment of society and their representatives are listened to and treated equally,” he said.He added: “It will be a chapter of statesmanship, respectful and substantive dialogue, and fulfilling the Knesset’s role as an effective and strong oversight body—an important and critical role in these sensitive times. Matan—I am proud of you and confident in your success.”However, Netanyahu strongly criticised the election. In a statement issued on behalf of Likud, he said: “A disgrace for all eternity. Tonight, a Knesset Speaker was appointed unilaterally with the votes of terror supporters. This is a low point in the Knesset’s history.”“The people of Israel oppose handing the keys to the country’s government to those who disgrace the national anthem. The people of Israel yearn for unity. Eisenkot, Bennett and Lieberman chose terror supporters over national unity today. History will remember this,” he added.Yair Lapid also endorsed Kahana’s appointment, calling it an important step towards repairing Israel’s political divisions.“Matan Kahana, Speaker of the Knesset. I am proud of him and confident that he will fulfil his role in a way that brings honour to Israel’s parliament. His election is an important step toward repairing and healing Israel,” Lapid said.The speakership carries considerable influence in Israel’s 120-member, unicameral parliament, including authority over the legislative agenda and the progression of bills. Kahana’s appointment could help the Eisenkot-led bloc advance proposals for an independent inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, term limits for the prime minister and the repeal of judicial changes introduced by Netanyahu’s previous government.Government formation remains uncertainDespite its parliamentary gains, Eisenkot faces difficulties in forming a government. His Yashar-led bloc and partners hold 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties has 53. Arab parties, which hold 19 seats, could provide crucial support.President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot with forming the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker Prime Minister until a new administration is established. If negotiations fail, Israel could face another election next year.You use AI every day. articles.title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
articles.summary: The $60m (£45m) plane was destroyed in an hours-long raid by an anti-war protester, according to the FBI.
articles.body:
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly snuck onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.

Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.

American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.

"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."

Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.

He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.

"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.

He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.

He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

The US charges say that he had planned well, because he avoided cutting a line that would have risked causing massive explosion.

According to the Limerick Post , O'Corrain is from Cork City. Supporters have described him as an anti-war activist.

Shannon Airport is a key hub for US military personnel, and is frequently the scene of anti-war protests. It was used by President Donald Trump in September for his visit to Ireland.

US prosecutors note that there have been several breaches there in recent years by protesters, including in May 2025 when three people drove a van through a perimeter fence , and then again later that month when a US airplane was sprayed with paint, making it temporarily inoperable.

articles.summary: A property sale in Vermont eventually turned into a complicated legal dispute involving an unfinished pond, timber removed from private land, unpaid
articles.body: A property sale in Vermont eventually turned into a complicated legal dispute involving an unfinished pond, timber removed from private land, unpaid construction work and an alleged assault. What began as a business arrangement between two men expanded into a lawsuit involving a subcontractor, competing financial claims and allegations of extortion. After a jury awarded money to all three parties on different claims, the case reached the state's highest court.The Vermont Supreme Court, in its November 13, 2026, decision in Lamson v. Goode, available on Justia, upheld the lower court's judgment in all respects. The ruling preserved awards of $15,100 for civil extortion in favour of subcontractor Chase Locke, $7,500 for breach of contract in favour of Gregory Lamson and $5,000 for assault in favour of James Goode. The court also upheld the decision to deny attorney's fees to both Lamson and Goode under Vermont's Prompt Pay Act.A land sale led to a dispute over pond constructionThe dispute began in 2015, when Lamson sold 42 acres of land in Royalton, Vermont, to Goode. Following the sale, Goode hired Lamson to construct a pond on another property he owned. Lamson subcontracted Locke to clear-cut the land for the proposed pond. Separately, Lamson also hired Locke to cut timber on his own property. However, disagreements developed over payments, the completion of the pond project and the use of equipment. Lamson eventually filed a lawsuit against both men in 2017.He accused Goode of breaching their construction agreement by preventing him from completing the pond and refusing to pay him. He also alleged that Goode had wrongfully used his tractor and prevented him from accessing a crane and other personal belongings left at the Royalton property. Against Locke, Lamson brought claims involving breach of contract and conversion, alleging that the subcontractor had sold timber and firewood from his property.The defendants also filed counterclaims. Goode accused Lamson of assault, among other allegations, while Locke claimed that Lamson had failed to pay him for logging work and threatened to make false police reports to obtain money and property.Jury awarded money on three separate claimsFollowing a jury trial, the court entered judgment in favour of Lamson on his breach-of-contract claim against Goode, awarding him $7,500, along with $8,149.32 in prejudgment interest. However, Goode also received $5,000 on his assault claim, while Locke was awarded $15,100 on his civil extortion claim. The extortion allegations centred on claims that Lamson had repeatedly threatened to report Locke to the police and his parole officer unless he handed over money and valuable property, including a storage locker. Locke argued that the threats were intended to obtain something from him through coercion.Lamson challenged the legal basis for the civil extortion claim, arguing that Vermont's criminal extortion law did not create a separate civil right to sue. The trial court initially agreed but later reconsidered its decision and allowed the claim to go before the jury. Both Lamson and Goode also sought attorney's fees under Vermont's Prompt Pay Act, which provides for fees when a party substantially prevails in a payment dispute involving construction work. The trial court denied both requests, finding that neither had achieved a sufficiently decisive victory.Why the Vermont Supreme Court upheld the awardsLamson and Goode appealed different parts of the judgment. Goode argued that he should have received attorney's fees because Lamson had not established a violation of the Prompt Pay Act. Lamson also sought fees and challenged Locke's $15,100 extortion award. The Supreme Court concluded that deciding whether a party substantially prevailed was within the trial court's discretion. It found that neither Lamson nor Goode had achieved the kind of comparative victory necessary to qualify for attorney's fees.On the extortion issue, the justices found that Vermont precedent allowed the recovery of money or property transferred under economic duress. The jury had been instructed to award Locke the value of money or property he had handed over to Lamson, making the award consistent with restitution principles. The justices therefore upheld the $15,100 award without deciding whether Vermont law recognises a separate civil cause of action for extortion. The court also noted that Lamson had failed to preserve his challenge to the amount of damages through a timely post-trial motion and had not ordered a transcript of the relevant trial testimony.On November 13, 2026, the Vermont Supreme Court affirmed the judgment in its entirety. The decision left all three monetary awards intact and denied both parties' requests for attorney's fees.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
articles.summary: The Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson "because he's already so famous".
articles.body:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well-known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first Bond film in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

articles.title: Irish man allegedly used axe, chemicals to destroy $60 million US military aircraft
articles.summary: A 48-year-old Irish man has been charged in the United States with destroying a $60 million American military aircraft after allegedly breaking into it at
articles.body: A 48-year-old Irish man has been charged in the United States with destroying a $60 million American military aircraft after allegedly breaking into it at Shannon Airport in Ireland and causing extensive damage with an axe, chemicals and other tools.An indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, also known as David Curran, with destruction of US government property over the April 11 incident. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.According to US prosecutors, O'Corrain breached the airport's security perimeter at around 4.40 am and entered a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked on a taxiway. The aircraft was en route to another country for a military assignment.Prosecutors said he destroyed its locking mechanism to gain access and then barricaded himself inside. He allegedly used straps, brackets and screws to secure the doors, while placing ball bearings mixed with epoxy in the door tracks to prevent them from opening or closing.Over the following hours, O'Corrain allegedly cut wire bundles and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and smashed every gauge in the cockpit. He also used an axe to damage the aircraft's exterior and poured substances and objects, including ball bearings, into its fuel tanks.The aircraft was rendered inoperable and will not return to active flight status, US prosecutors said. The plane was worth approximately $60 million.Months of planning allegedUS prosecutors said O'Corrain had researched the aircraft and planned the attack for months. He allegedly searched online for information about the construction of the C-130 and coordinates that could help him enter the airport grounds without detection.He also subscribed to a mobile application providing live flight tracking, including information about military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors said.The indictment further alleged that he attempted to contact someone who had previously been involved in a security breach at Shannon Airport.“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” James Barnacle, head of the FBI's New York office, said in a statement.According to the BBC, FBI officials said O'Corrain had acquired tools and materials and prepared to maximise the damage he could inflict. Prosecutors also alleged that he avoided cutting a particular line because doing so could have risked causing an explosion.The aircraft's crew returned to the airport after resting elsewhere and spotted O'Corrain through the uncovered cockpit windshield at around 9.40 am, according to the indictment. They alerted security.Crew members then saw him emerge through a roof hatch and swing an axe at the aircraft's exterior. Images included in the indictment showed a man standing on top of the plane.O'Corrain was arrested at the scene by Ireland's police force, An Garda Siochana, and was charged there with criminal damage and trespassing.Suspect not in US custodyO'Corrain is not currently in US custody, and an arraignment on the new charge has not been scheduled. The indictment said he was expected to be brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York. Online court records do not list an attorney who could speak on his behalf.Manhattan US Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sent “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated.”The FBI said the attack had jeopardised critical military operations.O'Corrain's supporters have described him as an independent peace activist. An online fundraiser organised by people identifying themselves as his friends and comrades said he had damaged the aircraft in protest against US involvement in the war with Iran and its support for Israel's war in Gaza.“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war support of Israel's genocide,” fundraiser organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.Shannon Airport, in western Ireland, is an international gateway and a hub for American troops and military equipment. It was also used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September.The airport has experienced several security breaches in recent years. According to the BBC, three people drove a van through its perimeter fence in May 2025, while another incident that month involved three people accused of spray-painting a US military aircraft, temporarily rendering it inoperable. The latest incident adds to that record of breaches at the airport.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US midterms: Alaska turns blue as Peltola defeats Sullivan, seals 56-44 Democratic Senate majority
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska's US Senate race, flipping the ninth Republican-held seat to her
articles.body: Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska's US Senate race, flipping the ninth Republican-held seat to her party and giving Democrats a 56-44 majority in the chamber when the new Congress begins in January.The victory marks the Democrats' biggest midterm Senate gain in nearly 70 years. The party last gained nine or more seats in a midterm election in 1958, when it captured 15 seats during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower's second term, according to historical US election data cited by AP.Peltola secured 50 per cent of first-preference votes against Sullivan's 46 per cent, clearing the threshold required to win outright under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, projections by US media showed.Her victory came despite Alaska voting for US president Donald Trump by 13 percentage points in 2024. Voter concerns over the rising cost of living, along with the state's independent political streak, helped make the contest competitive.In a post on X after media projected her victory, Peltola said, "As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.""Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work," she added.The campaign's final stretch was overshadowed by allegations that Democrats had helped recruit an independent candidate, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, to split votes and confuse supporters of the Republican incumbent. Republican Gerry Heikes was also on the general-election ballot.Republicans sought to remove Sullivan Jr., arguing that he was not a "good faith" candidate. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected the challenge.The New York Times reported shortly before Election Day that Peltola's campaign had helped recruit Sullivan Jr. Her campaign denied involvement. Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation, saying it was examining anything that could "resemble perjury".The Justice Department also opened a criminal investigation. US attorney general Todd Blanche described the reported recruitment effort as "fraud". Reuters previously reported that the department had issued more than 140 subpoenas, letters and notices in the probe, though these actions do not establish wrongdoing.Peltola's victory was the final Senate race to be called, completing nine Republican-held seat flips. Democrats had already secured their eighth pickup with Scott Colom's victory in Mississippi.The party also reclaimed the House of Representatives, gaining 42 seats as of Tuesday.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 13-year-old boy travelled from South Africa to England for a five-day visit but stayed beyond his return date; a year later, the Court of Appeal dismissed appeals by both him and his father, upholding the order sending him back
articles.summary: A boy then 13 was living with his mother in South Africa when he travelled to England on 15 October 2025 to spend five days with his father during his
articles.body: A boy then 13 was living with his mother in South Africa when he travelled to England on 15 October 2025 to spend five days with his father during his school half-term holiday. He was due to return on 20 October but did not board his flight. Shortly before the flight, his father informed the boy’s mother that he would not be returning. The mother subsequently applied under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention, seeking his return to South Africa.According to the Court of Appeal judgment dated 30 April 2026, the High Court ordered his return on 24 February 2026. His father and the boy both appealed, arguing against the decision. However, the Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals and upheld the return order.How did a visit to England turn into an international child abduction caseThe boy, identified in the judgment as X, was living with his mother in South Africa. She had been given permission to relocate there with him in 2018. His father began proceedings in South Africa in January 2025, seeking an order that X live with him in England.On 15 October 2025, when he was 13, X travelled to England for a five-day visit during the school half-term holiday. He was due to return to South Africa on 20 October 2025 but did not board his flight. Shortly before the scheduled departure, his father wrote a letter to the mother informing her that X would not be returning. On 23 October 2025, the mother applied under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention for X’s return to South Africa.What did the psychological report reveal about the father's parentingThe father opposed a return order, relying on X’s objections and on Article 13(b), the latter based broadly on security concerns and the alleged risk of crime in South Africa. The parties accepted that X objected to returning and was then sufficiently mature for his views to be properly considered.The High Court rejected the Article 13(b) defence but had to decide whether to exercise its discretion to order a return. The judge concluded that the father’s concerns fell short of the required threshold. He examined the strength and authenticity of X’s objections, including whether they reflected the teenager’s own views or had been influenced by his father. On 24 February 2026, the judge ordered that 14-year-old X be returned to South Africa under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention.As part of the father's legal proceedings in South Africa, a clinical psychologist was asked to conduct a psychological assessment of the family. The report was dated 23 June 2025 and ran to 159 pages. The psychologist carried out extensive inquiries, which included travelling to England and interviewing a significant number of people. Her report contained a detailed analysis and reached several conclusions about the family, some of which were later considered by the UK court.The father disputed the report's findings and submitted several documents challenging its accuracy. These included witness statements from seven people interviewed by the psychologist, who claimed that she had misrepresented or inaccurately recorded their statements. He also submitted an evaluation by another clinical psychologist, who reviewed the June 2025 report and raised several criticisms and concerns about its contents.The psychological report contained a detailed assessment of the father's parenting style and behaviour. It presented a strong criticism of his approach to parenting, which the judge described as a “blistering critique”.Father challenged findings on psychological report and paternal influenceBoth the father and X appealed the High Court decision. X argued that the judge had carried out a flawed assessment and had not properly considered the impact of returning him against his wishes. His appeal challenged a case management decision and reliance on a psychological report prepared for the South African proceedings.The father argued that the judge had given insufficient consideration to X’s objections and had wrongly treated them as the product of paternal influence. He disputed the handling of the evidence, including the psychologist’s report, and said the judge had not adequately considered X’s welfare. The father maintained that X wanted to remain in England and raised concerns about the risks of returning him to South Africa.Court rejects appeals and confirms boy's return to South AfricaThe Court of Appeal said the judge had considered X’s objections and explained why he regarded them as significantly influenced by his father. It found that the judge was entitled to rely on the June 2025 psychological report and reject the guardian’s recommendation against a return order.The appeal court concluded that the judge had balanced the possible consequences of making and not making the order. It said the evidence did not establish a grave risk of psychological harm or an intolerable situation in South Africa. The court found convincing evidence of a carefully planned abduction in this particular case. Lord Justices Newey and Dove agreed with Lord Justice Moylan. Both appeals were dismissed, leaving the return order in place.Disclaimer: This article is based on the Court of Appeal judgment in Re X (A Child), delivered on 30 April 2026. The Times of India has not independently verified the evidence or allegations presented by either parent. The claims, arguments and findings mentioned in this article are reported as recorded in the court judgment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Human' is the Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year
articles.summary: The growth of AI means we need to say when something is made by humans, says the book's editor.
articles.body:
"Human" is the Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year — defined as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines".

"The growth of AI means it is now necessary to explicitly say 'human' for things that once could only be done by humans," said chief editor Colin McIntosh.

Examples of current usage included actors Scarlett Johansson challenging "an assault on human creativity" and Matthew McConaughey protecting himself against unauthorised digital reproduction of his voice or image.

"The measure of AI's success should be how much it improves human lives," said Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates on learning about the dictionary's choice.

McIntosh said dictionary editors had to be on top of how words could change over time "to reflect what people say and what they write".

His research revealed a four-fold use of the word human since 1900.

"'Man' used to be used in this sense a lot more, but now it is not acceptable to use 'man' to mean men and women," he added.

"Human didn't come into use in Middle English until the 14th Century, from a French word. Shakespeare used it, but after that it was very restricted in use."

There had also been an increased use of compound words such as human-made and human-driven, to distinguish the works, qualities and skills of people from AI.

"Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking has made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI, from top mathematicians to teachers of young children," said McIntosh.

Gates recently made the case for "human reserved jobs" , such as caregiving, and reiterated his call for a robot tax to help fund training for people who lose their jobs to AI.

Other examples included the Nobel Prize in Physics laureate Geoffrey Hinton, who has been described as the godfather of AI, who warned "we're creating alien beings. I'm willing to be selfish and choose humans".

Pope Leo XIV has spoken of new forms of "dehumanisation" and the "pressing duty to remain profoundly human".

"Right now our understanding of humanity is changing," said Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge.

"We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart? Is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?"

In response to the surge in AI-created content , academics are hoping to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made", similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s.

Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: "AI brings us back to questions that we've asked for millennia — who are we? What does it mean to be human?

"AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There's a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."

articles.title: MacKenzie Scott gave away $26 billion without asking for donations to be named after her, letting charities decide how to spend the money, while four wealthy donors put $189 million into democracy institutes bearing their names
articles.summary: MacKenzie Scott has given away more than $26 billion since 2019, making her one of America's most prominent philanthropists.
articles.body: MacKenzie Scott has given away more than $26 billion since 2019, making her one of America's most prominent philanthropists. Her approach to charitable giving, however, differs from that of many wealthy donors. Rather than directing how recipients should use their money or seeking recognition through institutions named after her, Scott generally makes unrestricted donations, allowing organisations to decide where the funds are most needed. A different approach has emerged among some of America's biggest donors to democracy programmes. Four wealthy donor families have collectively contributed $189 million to university institutes carrying their names. A new investigation by The Chronicle of Philanthropy examines these contrasting approaches and the growing flow of private wealth into American democracy research and education.Democracy programmes receive $369.2 million in major donationsAccording to The Chronicle of Philanthropy, wealthy donors made 18 gifts worth at least $1 million each to democracy programmes between 2006 and 2025. These contributions amounted to a combined $369.2 million, with many of the publicly announced donations going to university institutes and centres focused on democracy, government and public policy.The funding increased considerably in recent years. Around $266.5 million, representing 72% of the total, was donated between 2021 and 2025. Contributions peaked in 2024, when democracy programmes received $84 million.Universities emerged as the biggest beneficiaries, receiving approximately four out of every five dollars donated during the period. Three of the gifts identified by the Chronicle went to other organisations, including the American Civil Liberties Union, Interfaith America and New York Historical.The four largest donations alone accounted for $189 million, with each going towards a university institute carrying the benefactors' names.The four wealthy donors behind $189 million in donationsThe largest contribution came from Leonard Schaeffer and his late wife, Pamela, who donated $59 million to the University of Southern California in 2024. The money established the Leonard D. Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy & Government Service, a research and education centre headquartered at USC's Capital Campus in Washington, DC.Leonard Schaeffer founded health insurer WellPoint and is a professor of public policy at USC. He previously served as administrator of the Health Care Financing Administration during the administration of former US President Jimmy Carter. His name was already associated with the university through a 2009 donation that established the USC Schaeffer Center for Health Policy & Economics, which now houses the new institute.The second-largest contribution came from Francis and Kathleen Rooney, who donated $55 million to the University of Notre Dame in 2025 to endow the Rooney Democracy Institute. The institution was previously known as the Rooney Center for the Study of American Democracy, established in 2008 through the couple's foundation.Francis Rooney is a Republican who represented Florida's Fort Myers area in the US House of Representatives from 2017 to 2021. He previously served as CEO of investment and holding company Rooney Holdings Inc.The University of Virginia received $50 million from Bruce Karsh, co-founder of investment management firm Oaktree Capital Management, and his wife, Martha, in 2021. Both are alumni of the university's law school. Their contribution established the Karsh Institute of Democracy, with UVA announcing plans to match the donation.In 2022, the John Nau III Foundation contributed another $15 million to endow the institute, taking the university's total donations identified in the Chronicle's tally to $65 million, the highest among the recipients.The fourth major contribution came from Richard and Nancy Kinder, who donated $25 million to the University of Missouri in 2022 to expand the Kinder Institute on Constitutional Democracy. The latest contribution brought their total donations to the institute to approximately $60 million. Their foundation first endowed the institution in 2015. Richard Kinder is the co-founder of energy infrastructure company Kinder Morgan and earned his undergraduate and law degrees from the University of Missouri.MacKenzie Scott's different approach to philanthropyUnlike donors who establish or expand institutions bearing their names, Scott generally gives organisations unrestricted funding, allowing them to determine how the money should be allocated.Her donations are made through Yield Giving, which identifies potential recipients through its own research and assessment process rather than relying exclusively on conventional grant applications. The organisations receiving the money are generally free to use it for their operational needs, programmes, staffing, infrastructure or other priorities.One example is Democracy Works, the nonprofit organisation behind TurboVote, a voter-engagement platform that helps Americans navigate voter registration and elections.In 2023, Democracy Works announced that it had received an unrestricted donation from Scott, describing it as the largest single contribution in the organisation's history. Its CEO, Luis Lozada, said the funding would provide a strong foundation for the organisation to continue innovating.The organisation did not have to establish an institute or programme carrying Scott's name in return for the donation. It was selected through Yield Giving's research process.Scott's approach is widely associated with trust-based philanthropy, which places greater responsibility on recipient organisations to decide how best to use the money rather than requiring donors to prescribe specific spending priorities.Her donations extend beyond democracy programmesScott's hands-off approach is not limited to organisations working on elections or democratic institutions. Her philanthropy spans education, healthcare, environmental protection, housing and other social causes.The Bob Woodruff Foundation, which supports military veterans, service members and their families, is another major recipient. Scott donated $15 million to the organisation in 2022, followed by another $20 million in 2025, bringing her contributions to $35 million.The foundation's CEO, Anne Marie Dougherty, has described Scott's approach as trust-based philanthropy.Education has also been a major focus of Scott's giving. She has donated more than $1 billion to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), supporting institutions that have historically faced funding disparities.Healthcare has similarly featured prominently in her philanthropic work. According to a Harvard Business School study cited by Fortune, healthcare was Yield Giving's largest category by absolute donation value in 2023.Democracy remains a small part of overall philanthropic givingDespite the substantial contributions made by wealthy donors to democracy-focused institutions, the sector continues to account for a relatively small share of their overall philanthropy.The Chronicle's investigation found that education and healthcare remain major priorities for many wealthy donors, with democracy-related contributions representing only a portion of their charitable spending.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: The heavy-footed herd helping conservation in the Lake District
articles.summary: A herd of "hardy" Belted Galloways and Luings help trample dominant grasses in the Swindale Valley.
articles.body:
As the season's first snow cloaks the Lake District fells, there is one particular herd of cows thriving in the frosty weather.

The herd of 53 "hardy" Scottish-bred Belted Galloways and Luings have roamed RSPB's Wild Haweswater for some years, emulating the wild herbivores before the bronze age, as part of a conservation grazing project.

The large, heavy-footed animals trample denser, more dominant vegetation allowing delicate plants and young trees to grow, its site manager Glen Swainson said.

The growth of trees is increasingly important for the area, with them slowing down the flow of water to help reduce flood and drought risk and providing valuable shelter to Swindale's livestock.

"Their short legs mean they are low to the ground which, along with their thick, double coat and wide back, means they are built to survive well in the uneven terrain and harsh weather we have here in the Lake District," he said.

Swainson said Haweswater's native flora and fauna had "evolved alongside the way these animals graze and trample, so native breeds bring lots of advantages when looking to restore habitats that are degraded".

He said their "long, agile tongues wrap around vegetation and tug at it" which also creates different heights of grasses and plants benefitting insects to small mammals, amphibians, reptiles and birds.

Similar schemes in southern Scotland and Berkshire use the cattle in efforts to restore rare heathland and to increase biodiversity.

In late summer, the Swindale wildflower meadows were cut to allow a "rich diversity of wildflowers and grasses to seed", which is placed to feed the cattle and Cumbrian fell ponies, which also work to trample grasses , in the "harshest winter weather".

Swainson said the hay was put down onto areas of "more dominant rushes and Bracken, which means the animals trample those areas as they feed".

The herd is often split up into smaller groups and is regularly moved so they do not overgraze a particular patch, he said.

articles.title: Kent fire service battery disposal plea after waste site fires
articles.summary: Kent fire service raises awareness of how to dispose of batteries and rechargeable electrical items.
articles.body:
People are being urged to dispose of batteries and electrical items responsibly after a series of fires at waste dumps in the past year.

Kent Fire and Rescue Service (KFRS) is campaigning to raise awareness of how to dispose of batteries and rechargeable electrical items to reduce the risk of a fire.

Firefighters said battery-related fires were often caused by items such as electric toothbrushes and razors, vapes and household batteries being disposed of incorrectly.

Kent councillor Jamie Henderson said batteries and small electricals that were not disposed of correctly had caused 22 fires at Kent's waste and recycling facilities and 139 at the Allington Energy from Waste plant.

He said a battery might seem small but could have "serious consequences" when thrown into a household bin.

Station manager Kev Chapman said people should not put them in their general household waste or recycling.

He urged people to dispose of items safely, adding: "By doing so, we can help prevent large fires and protect the lives of our crews and waste operatives."

Chapman said: "If a battery or rechargeable item gets wet, damaged or crushed, there is a risk it could overheat and catch alight, which has been the cause of previous fires involving waste and recycling sites and vehicles.

"These fires can be avoided if people dispose of their batteries and rechargeable electrical items in the right way."

James Farquhar, regional manager for waste service provider Suez South East, said vapes and batteries that had been disposed of incorrectly, particularly lithium-ion batteries, were a leading cause of fires in waste facilities and vehicles.

"Once a fire starts, it can spread rapidly through the different materials being processed, making it challenging to control and creating significant risks," he said.

The fire service campaign has been backed by councils, waste service providers and other organisations.

Information on where to dispose of electrical items and batteries can be found on the KFRS website .

articles.title: Canadian communities are turning around 18,000 discarded tyres into accessible playgrounds; 11 projects will use recycled rubber to create safer public spaces

articles.body: Communities across British Columbia, Canada, are giving discarded tyres a new purpose by turning them into safer and more accessible playgrounds and recreation spaces. Through the 2026 Community Grant Program run by Tire Stewardship BC (TSBC), 11 projects will collectively reuse 17,828 recycled tyres to improve public facilities for children and people with different mobility needs. The initiative includes playground upgrades, resurfacing work and recreation improvements, showing how waste materials can be put to practical use while making shared community spaces more inclusive.Nearly 18,000 recycled tyres are creating accessible playgroundsAccording to Tire Stewardship BC, the organisation announced the 11 recipients of its 2026 Community Grant Program on June 4, 2026. The funding will support 10 playground projects and one community centre, with the aim of creating more inclusive public spaces using recycled tyres collected in British Columbia.The programme is designed to help communities introduce or complete projects that might otherwise face difficulties securing funding for accessibility improvements. Rather than allowing old tyres to become waste, the initiative puts their recycled rubber to use in places where children and families gather.The 17,828 tyres will be converted into surfacing and other recreation-related materials. One of the main advantages of rubber playground surfaces is that they provide a smoother and more stable area than loose materials such as wood chips or gravel. This makes it easier for wheelchair users, people with walkers and others who use mobility devices to move around playgrounds.The improvement is important for children who find traditional playground surfaces difficult to navigate. A more stable surface can help them reach play areas and participate in activities alongside their peers.11 projects bring improvements to communities across British ColumbiaThe 2026 grant recipients are spread across several communities, with projects ranging from complete playground replacements to smaller accessibility upgrades.North Vancouver has one of the largest projects on the list. The Board of Education of School District No. 44 received support for the new playground at Sherwood Park Elementary, which will use 4,256 recycled tyres. The City of Revelstoke's Kovach Park resurfacing project follows with 2,710 tyres allocated for the improvement.Whistler's Meadow Park Playground replacement will use 2,003 recycled tyres, while the Art Wilkinson Playground project in Port Moody has been allocated 1,683. Immaculate Conception School in Vancouver will use another 1,649 tyres for its school playground revitalisation.Other projects include the inclusive playground at École Robb Road in Comox, which will use 1,639 tyres, and the Spud Murphy Playground surfacing project in Abbotsford, which has been allocated 1,497.Campbell River will benefit from two separate initiatives. The Strathcona Regional District's Mitlenatch Park accessibility improvements will use 1,023 recycled tyres, while the Pinecrest Playground resurfacing project will use 494.The remaining allocations include 709 tyres for the BC Winter Games' gymnastics equipment and community arena matting initiative in Trail and Rossland, and 165 for improvements to the École Cobble Hill Elementary playground.Together, these projects account for all 17,828 recycled tyres included in the programme.A school playground project highlights the importance of inclusionOne of the projects has particular significance for families at École Cobble Hill Elementary. The school's Parent Advisory Council Society will use the grant to carry out a phased redevelopment of its playground, replacing ageing infrastructure and improving accessibility for students and their families.TSBC's announcement highlighted the experience of Vivienne Damatan, whose daughter lives with spinal muscular atrophy, a condition that affects muscle strength and mobility. For the family, the playground has been an important place for building friendships, confidence and independence.Damatan explained that improving accessibility would allow more children to enjoy those experiences alongside their peers. The project is intended to create an environment where children with different abilities can explore, play and develop social connections.The programme builds on decades of tyre recycling effortsThe community projects are part of a longer effort to find useful applications for discarded tyres. According to Tire Stewardship BC, British Columbia's scrap tyre recycling programme is the oldest in Canada and marked its 35th year in 2026. Since beginning in 1991, the programme has recycled more than 128 million tyres, turning them into products such as playground surfaces, walkways and fitness tracks.The TSBC Community Grant Program has also developed considerably over the years. Now in its 18th year, it has invested more than $6.84 million in 371 projects across 96 communities in British Columbia. The latest round adds another 11 projects to that record, with a particular focus on accessible play and recreation.The BC Winter Games initiative offers another example of how recycled rubber can serve different purposes. TSBC funded 256 recycled rubber mats to help secure gymnastics equipment during the Games held in February 2026. After the event, the mats were reused at the Rossland community arena, allowing the material to continue serving local recreational facilities.Recycled tyres offer benefits beyond playground constructionAccording to ARMA(Alberta Recycling Management Authority), discarded tyres can create several problems when they are not properly managed. They present a fire risk, and burning tyres can release toxic fumes. Tyres left outdoors can also collect standing water, creating conditions where insects and bacteria can multiply.Recycling provides an alternative by turning the material into useful products. ARMA reports that Alberta's tyre recycling programme, launched in 1992, has helped recycle more than 1.66 million tonnes of tyres.
